newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Italian foreign minister urges global landmine ban.
newsitem.headline: Italian foreign minister urges global landmine ban.

text.p: Italian Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini appealed on Tuesday for a global treaty to be agreed within two years banning anti-personnel landmines which kill and cripple thousands of civilians annually.
Dini, in a speech opening the 1997 session of the Conference on Disarmament, proposed that as a first step, an international register recording all exports of landmines should be created.
He also urged reviving stalled talks on halting production of nuclear bomb-making material, the so-called fissile cut-off negotiations on plutonium and highly enriched plutonium.

The Geneva Conference agreed in March 1995 to negotiate a treaty to halt production of fissile material, but the talks never got off the ground as negotiations for Comprehensive Test Ban Treaty (CTBT) banning underground blasts took precedence.
"Priority must be given to emergency situations, and the main emergency the international community is required to deal with today is the question of anti-personnel landmines," Dini said.
"We must focus on this issue for moral and humanitarian reasons and also in the interest of economic development."
Dini called for the 61-member body to concentrate on resuscitating negotiations to halt fissile production and to push ahead with a ban on landmines.
"I believe the two matters could go in parallel," he told a news conference. "...I think there will be consensus, broad agreement to go ahead on the two issues."
The United States said on Friday that it would observe a unilateral ban on the export of landmines and would push for a global ban to be clinched at the Geneva conference.

There are some 100 million landmines sown worldwide which kill or maim an estimated 25,000 civilians a year, including thousands of children, according to the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) which has long campaigned for a ban.
Britain's Diana, Princess of Wales, called for an international ban on the "hideous weapons" when she visited Angola last week and met casualties of its 20-year civil war.
France and Britain have backed negotiations in Geneva on landmines, but major states using landmines, including China, Russia and India, have been reluctant, according to envoys.
Dini, asked how long it would take the United-Nations sponsored body to negotiate a ban on anti-personnel landmines, replied: "In my view, it shouldn't take long.
"It was a miracle that the Comprehensive Test Ban Treaty could be completed in two years. I think the landmine situation is a simpler issue, in my own view, and should take less than that," he added.

But the Geneva body remains divided over its 1997 agenda, according to its chairman, South Korea's ambassador Joun Yung Sun. "Unfortunately, I must report that the Conference has yet to reach a consensus on the agenda and work program," he said.

India and Pakistan are leading the non-aligned countries in pushing for the five declared nuclear powers (Britain, China, France, Russia and the United States) to agree to negotiate total nuclear disarmament within a defined timetable.
Only then would the non-aligned be prepared to push ahead on cut-off as part of an overall package, according to diplomats.
"I don't think things will move soon on cut-off, given the position of India and Pakistan, who are by no means isolated," a Western disarmament negotiator told Reuters.
